MACROETCH METHOD FOR TEST FOR TITANIUM ALLOYS

0.1 This Indian Standard was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards on 18 April 1988, after the draft finalized by the Heat Treatment and Metallography Sectional Committee had been approved by the Structural and Metals Division Council. 0.2 Macroetch test method is frequently used as evaluating technique for revealing solidification segregation, general distribution and structure, size of inclusions, porosity, grain size, flow lines, manufacturing defects and surface condition, It is done by etching a method of manufacture. suitably prepared specimen and examining it

1. SCOPE 1.1 Macroetching is the etching of specimen for examination at low magnifications and is used to reveal the macrostructure of titanium alloys such as bar, billets, forgings and products, The present procedure is intended to castings. be followed for classifying titanium alloys by a graded series showing the characteristic structure and incidence of certain processing defects. This method is limited in application to titanium alloy billets, forgings and castings. 2. SIGNIFICANCE 2.1 Macroetching is a simple test which provides information about the heterogeneity of the sample. It will show: (a) variation In structure such as structure; (b) presence grain size and columnar of acute segregation and banding, and (c) the presence of discontinuities, such as laps, seam5 and bursts. 3. SAMPLING

However, the sample should not be taken so early that further working The sample is can introduce serious defects. uslual!v taken after ingot breakdown and after Billets or most chances of bursts have passed. blooms going into small sizes are sampled after Materials going into forging initial breakdown. billets or other -products are sampled at near finish size. Sampling may be done systematically on a random basis.

methods

are

3.1.1.1 Billets, blooms and hot-rolled products Discs are usually cut from these products near the end but fish tails should be avoided. Discs from large blooms can be cut into smaller pieces. 3.1.2 Forgings and l?~trusion - Discs, cut transverse to the long dimension, are used to see bursts, voids, etc. Forging can be cut parallel to long dimensions to show flow lines. Macroetching of an unprepared specimen shows surface defects, such as shuts, flats, seams, etc. 3.1.3 Sheets and Plates - While looking for defects in sheets, as large a sample as possible should be taken. When seeking information on lamination, a transverse section is used. 3.1.4 Weldrnents - A disc perpendicular to direction of welding shows weld penetration, heat affected zone, structure, etc. 3.1.5 Castings - Specimen different regions depending sought. should be cut from upon the features

3.2 When macroetching is used to solve a problem, then the problem itself largely dictates the sample location on the work piece and the stage of manufacture; for example, when looking for pipe, the sample should represent the top to A,-_ :___a ^_ . ..L-- luoKmg 1--1X..- J?LL,~: ~lbg:or, ~1 WII~II Iur 1-.. uurst, the sampie should be taken as soon after hot working as possible. 3.3 Sample may be cold cut by any convenient means. Saw and abrasive cut off wheels and EDS cutting are particularly effective. Since 1

IS r 12378- 1988 heat generation during abrasive cutting may affect the structure of the sample, the surface to be examined should be at least 10 mm away from cut surface in case of EDS cutting and 3 mm in case of abrasive cutting. 4. SPECIMEN PREPARATION Mixing hood. and etching should be done in a fume

6. PROCEDURE 6.1 The specimen may be etched by immersion The time of or by swabbing or by both means. etching will vary depending upon the composition, size and structural condition. Generally speaking 30 s to 10 min will be sufficient. Over-etching can lead to misinterpretation and hence light Table 1 gives the time for etching is better. various etchants, but should be used as a guide only. After etching, specimen should be washed in running water and blown dry with compressed air. 7. EXAMINATION OF SPECIMENS

4.1 Sample preparation need not be elaborate. Any method of presenting a smooth surface with a minimum amount of cold work will be satisfactory. Discs may be faced on a lathe or shaper. The usual procedure is to take a roughing cut, then a finish cut. This will generate a smooth surface and remove cold work from prior operations. Grinding may also be employed using a fine wheel and light finished cuts. When fine detail is required, the specimen should be finished with metallographic paper. 4.2 After surface preparation, the sample shall be cleaned carefully with suitable solvents. Any greasr, oil or other residue left on the surface will produce uneven attack during macroetching. Therefore, care should be taken not to touch the sample surface or contaminate it in any other way after it has been cleaned. 5. SOLUTIONS 5.1 The most common solutions for macroetching titanium alloys are given in Table 1. 5.2 Caution must be observed acids as they are strong and can burns, The acid should be added

Therefore, the basis of macroetching inspection w~ill be a matter of agreement between the manufacturer and the purchaser, if this technique is being used as a quality test.
